title: What is the Circuit Breaker pattern, how does Resilience4j implement it, how does it differ from Retry, and what is the default aspect-order gotcha (Retry wrapping CircuitBreaker, `CallNotPermittedException`)?
shortTitle: What is the Circuit Breaker pattern, how does Resilience4j implement it, how does it differ from Retry, and what is the default aspect-order gotcha

s1_definition.profdef: The Circuit Breaker pattern is a stability mechanism that stops a service from repeatedly calling a dependency that is failing, by tracking the recent failure rate and, once it crosses a threshold, opening the circuit so further calls fail fast instead of hanging. Resilience4j implements it as a state machine with CLOSED, OPEN, and HALF_OPEN states driven by a sliding window of call outcomes, exposed through the `@CircuitBreaker` annotation or a functional decorator. Retry is a different pattern that simply re-attempts a failed call a few times with backoff. The default aspect-order gotcha is that when both are applied, Retry wraps CircuitBreaker, so Retry sees the circuit breaker's own `CallNotPermittedException` as just another failure and keeps retrying against an open circuit, which is usually not what you want.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's app calls an external credit-score service. If that service is down, calling it again and again just wastes time and ties up threads while every customer waits. A circuit breaker is like a smart fuse: after it sees too many failures it trips and immediately says "do not even try right now", so customers get a fast fallback instead of a long hang, and after a cooling-off period it cautiously lets one call through to test if the service recovered. Retry is a different idea, simply trying again two or three times for a brief hiccup. The gotcha is that if you stack them in the default order, the retry logic treats the tripped fuse itself as a failure and keeps hammering a fuse that has already said "stop".

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Circuit Breaker pattern is a stability mechanism that stops a service from repeatedly calling a dependency that is failing, by tracking the recent failure rate and, once it crosses a threshold, opening the circuit so further calls fail fast instead of hanging. Resilience4j implements it as a state machine with CLOSED, OPEN, and HALF_OPEN states driven by a sliding window of call outcomes, exposed through the `@CircuitBreaker` annotation or a functional decorator. Retry is a different pattern that simply re-attempts a failed call a few times with backoff. The default aspect-order gotcha is that when both are applied, Retry wraps CircuitBreaker, so Retry sees the circuit breaker's own `CallNotPermittedException` as just another failure and keeps retrying against an open circuit, which is usually not what you want.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's app calls an external credit-score service. If that service is down, calling it again and again just wastes time and ties up threads while every customer waits. A circuit breaker is like a smart fuse: after it sees too many failures it trips and immediately says "do not even try right now", so customers get a fast fallback instead of a long hang, and after a cooling-off period it cautiously lets one call through to test if the service recovered. Retry is a different idea, simply trying again two or three times for a brief hiccup. The gotcha is that if you stack them in the default order, the retry logic treats the tripped fuse itself as a failure and keeps hammering a fuse that has already said "stop".

**One line to remember:** A circuit breaker trips open after too many failures so calls fail fast, Resilience4j runs it as a CLOSED-OPEN-HALF_OPEN state machine over a sliding window, Retry just re-attempts, and by default Retry wraps CircuitBreaker so it retries the `CallNotPermittedException` of an open circuit unless you reorder them.

sections.s2_technical:
A circuit breaker exists to prevent a failing dependency from dragging down the caller. When a downstream service is slow or down, naive callers keep sending requests that each wait for a timeout, consuming threads and connections until the caller itself runs out of capacity and fails, which is how one failure cascades into a system-wide outage. The breaker watches outcomes and, once failures are frequent enough, it stops making calls for a while, letting the caller return instantly with a fallback and giving the struggling dependency room to recover.

Resilience4j models this as a three-state machine. In the CLOSED state calls pass through normally and outcomes are recorded in a sliding window, which can be count-based, say the last hundred calls, or time-based, say the last ten seconds. When the failure rate in that window crosses the configured threshold, for example fifty percent, the breaker transitions to OPEN. In the OPEN state every call is rejected immediately without touching the dependency, and the caller gets a `CallNotPermittedException` so it can run a fallback. After a configured wait duration the breaker moves to HALF_OPEN, where it permits a small number of trial calls; if those succeed it returns to CLOSED, and if they fail it goes back to OPEN. Resilience4j also supports a slow-call threshold, so calls that are too slow count as failures even if they technically succeed, which catches a dependency that is up but unhealthy.

Using it is straightforward. The declarative way is the annotation, `@CircuitBreaker(name = "creditScore", fallbackMethod = "fallbackScore")`, where the fallback method has the same signature plus the exception and returns a safe default. The functional way decorates a supplier: `Supplier<Score> decorated = CircuitBreaker.decorateSupplier(cb, () -> client.getScore(id));` and then you call `Try.ofSupplier(decorated).recover(ex -> defaultScore).get();`. The breaker's behaviour is tuned through its configuration: the window type and size, the failure-rate threshold, the wait duration in open state, the number of permitted calls in half-open, and the slow-call settings.

Retry is a separate, complementary pattern. It simply re-executes a failed call a bounded number of times, usually with a backoff such as exponential delay plus jitter, and optionally only for specific retryable exceptions. Retry is the right tool for a transient glitch, like a brief network blip or a momentary timeout, where trying again shortly will likely succeed. It is the wrong tool for a dependency that is genuinely down, because retrying just multiplies the load on something already failing. This is exactly why the two patterns are often combined: retry absorbs transient blips, and the circuit breaker protects against sustained failure.

The crucial gotcha is the aspect order when both annotations are on the same method. Resilience4j has a default order in which Retry is the outermost aspect and CircuitBreaker is inside it, meaning Retry wraps CircuitBreaker. The problem is that when the circuit is OPEN, the circuit breaker throws `CallNotPermittedException`, and because Retry is on the outside, Retry sees that exception as just another failed attempt and retries, which does nothing useful because the circuit is open and will keep rejecting. You end up retrying against a breaker that has already decided to fail fast, defeating the point of failing fast. The usual fix is to reverse the order so CircuitBreaker wraps Retry, which you do by configuring the aspect order so the circuit breaker is outermost; then a burst of retries counts as the attempts inside one logical call, and once the circuit opens, the whole thing fails fast immediately with no pointless retrying. Alternatively you configure Retry to ignore `CallNotPermittedException` so it does not retry an open circuit.

Senior nuances: always pair a circuit breaker with a timeout, because a breaker cannot trip on calls that never return; use a sensible fallback that is genuinely safe, like a cached or default value, not another risky call; size the window and thresholds to your traffic so the breaker is neither trigger-happy nor sluggish; and expose the breaker's state as a metric so operators can see when circuits open. Combine with a bulkhead to isolate thread pools so one slow dependency cannot exhaust shared threads.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's loan service calls an external credit-score provider. During an outage the provider stopped responding, and the loan service kept calling it, every call hanging on a timeout, until the loan service's threads were exhausted and it could not even serve requests that did not need a credit score. This is exactly what a circuit breaker prevents: after enough failures it trips open and the loan service fails fast with a safe fallback instead of hanging.

Problem 2 — Some failures were just brief network blips where an immediate retry would have succeeded. This is exactly the retry case, re-attempting a transient failure a couple of times.

Problem 3 — The team added both retry and circuit breaker and found that when the circuit opened, the service still took a long time because retry kept re-attempting the open circuit's rejection. This is exactly the aspect-order gotcha, where retry wrapping the circuit breaker retries `CallNotPermittedException`.

Our mini-project demonstrates all of this. The code defines a flaky `CreditScoreClient`, a simplified `CircuitBreaker` state machine with CLOSED, OPEN, and HALF_OPEN, a `Retrier`, and a demo that shows the circuit tripping open and failing fast, shows retry handling a transient blip, and demonstrates the wrong order retrying an open circuit versus the right order failing fast.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a credit-score provider that is currently down, and a loan service that calls it repeatedly for Rajesh's account.

Step 1: The first few calls go through the circuit breaker in the CLOSED state, reach the down provider, and fail with a timeout. The breaker counts these failures in its window.

Step 2: Once the consecutive failures cross the threshold, the breaker transitions to OPEN and records the time. From this point it stops calling the provider entirely.

Step 3: The next calls, while the breaker is OPEN, are rejected instantly with a `CallNotPermittedException`, so the loan service returns a safe fallback score immediately instead of hanging on a timeout. This frees threads and protects the service, which is the whole point.

Step 4: In the wrong aspect order, retry wraps the circuit breaker, so when the breaker throws `CallNotPermittedException` the retry logic treats it as a failed attempt and tries again two more times, each time hitting the open circuit and being rejected again, wasting effort and time against a circuit that has already decided to fail fast.

Step 5: In the right aspect order, the circuit breaker wraps retry, so when the circuit is OPEN the whole call fails fast immediately with zero wasted retries, and retry only ever runs inside a logical call to absorb a transient blip while the circuit is CLOSED. The output shows the circuit opening, the fast-fail fallback, and the contrast between the wasteful and correct orderings.

```
2026-10-24 14:46:50 SEVERE  call 1 failed: credit-score provider timeout
2026-10-24 14:46:50 SEVERE  call 4 failed: credit-score provider timeout
2026-10-24 14:46:50 WARNING circuit → OPEN after 4 failures
2026-10-24 14:46:50 WARNING call 5 FAST-FAIL (circuit OPEN) → fallback score=600
2026-10-24 14:46:50 WARNING call 6 FAST-FAIL (circuit OPEN) → fallback score=600
2026-10-24 14:46:50 SEVERE  wasted 3 retries against an OPEN circuit → CallNotPermittedException
2026-10-24 14:46:50 INFO    fast-fail immediately, zero wasted retries → fallback score=600
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Loan Service → credit-score call
    │
    ▼
  ┌──────────────── Circuit Breaker state machine ────────────────┐
  │  CLOSED ──(failure rate ≥ 50% in window)──▶ OPEN              │
  │    ▲                                          │ wait 5s        │
  │    │ trial calls succeed                       ▼                │
  │  HALF_OPEN ◀──(after waitDuration)──────────  (permit N trials)│
  │    │ trial fails → back to OPEN                                │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │ CLOSED/HALF_OPEN: real call           │ OPEN: reject fast
    ▼                                       ▼
  CreditScoreProvider (external)        CallNotPermittedException → fallback(600)

  ── Aspect order ──
  WRONG: Retry( CircuitBreaker ) → retries CallNotPermitted (wasteful)
  RIGHT: CircuitBreaker( Retry ) → OPEN fails fast ; Retry absorbs blips when CLOSED
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Circuit Breaker + Retry (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Circuit Breaker: state machine CLOSED/OPEN/HALF_OPEN         │
  │   WHY: fail fast under sustained failure, protect the caller │
  │ Retry: bounded re-attempt with backoff                       │
  │   WHY: absorb transient blips only                           │
  │ Decorator: wrap the supplier with resilience aspects         │
  │   WHY: compose timeout + breaker + retry + bulkhead cleanly  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: breaker tracks state; retrier re-attempts; client calls    │
  │ O: new resilience policy = new decorator, logic unchanged     │
  │ L: decorated supplier substitutes a plain supplier            │
  │ D: service depends on a Supplier abstraction                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Circuit Breaker ─────────────────────────────
  CLOSED ──failRate≥threshold──▶ OPEN ──waitDuration──▶ HALF_OPEN
    ▲                                                     │
    └──────── trial calls succeed ───────────────────────┘
                     trial fails ──────▶ back to OPEN

  ── Aspect-Order Decision ──────────────────────────────────────
  Retry(CircuitBreaker)?  → retries CallNotPermittedException → BAD
  CircuitBreaker(Retry)?  → OPEN fails fast, Retry only inside → GOOD
  Or: Retry.ignoreExceptions(CallNotPermittedException)

  ── Call Chain (right order) ───────────────────────────────────
  1. cb.call(() -> retry.run(() -> client.getScore(id)))
  2.   if OPEN → throw CallNotPermitted → fallback (fast, no retry)
  3.   if CLOSED → retry.run absorbs a blip, records outcome in window
  4.   window failRate ≥ threshold → OPEN
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Circuit Breaker pattern stops a service from repeatedly calling a dependency that is failing. When a downstream service is slow or down, a naive caller keeps sending requests that each wait for a timeout, consuming threads and connections until the caller itself runs out of capacity, which is how one failure cascades into a full outage. A circuit breaker watches recent outcomes and, once failures are frequent enough, it stops making calls for a while so the caller returns instantly with a fallback and the struggling dependency gets room to recover.

Resilience4j implements this as a three-state machine over a sliding window. In the CLOSED state calls pass through and outcomes are recorded in a count-based or time-based window. When the failure rate crosses the configured threshold, say fifty percent, it goes OPEN, and in the OPEN state every call is rejected immediately with a CallNotPermittedException so the caller runs its fallback. After a wait duration it moves to HALF_OPEN, where it allows a few trial calls; if they succeed it closes again, and if they fail it reopens. It also supports a slow-call threshold so a dependency that is up but unhealthy still trips the breaker. I use it through the CircuitBreaker annotation with a fallback method, or functionally by decorating a supplier.

Retry is a different, complementary pattern that simply re-executes a failed call a bounded number of times with backoff. It is the right tool for a transient glitch like a brief network blip, and the wrong tool for a dependency that is genuinely down, because retrying just multiplies load on something already failing. That is exactly why the two are combined: retry absorbs transient blips, and the circuit breaker protects against sustained failure.

The gotcha I always mention is the aspect order when both are on the same method. Resilience4j's default order makes Retry the outermost aspect wrapping CircuitBreaker, so when the circuit is OPEN and the breaker throws CallNotPermittedException, Retry sees that as just another failed attempt and keeps retrying against an open circuit, which wastes time and defeats the entire purpose of failing fast. On my loan service at National Bank of India, this made outages worse until we fixed it. The fix is to reverse the order so CircuitBreaker wraps Retry, by configuring the aspect order so the breaker is outermost, which means once the circuit opens the whole call fails fast with zero wasted retries and retry only runs inside a logical call while the circuit is closed. Alternatively I configure Retry to ignore CallNotPermittedException so it never retries an open circuit. I also always pair the breaker with a timeout, because a breaker cannot trip on calls that never return, use a genuinely safe fallback like a cached or default value, and expose the circuit state as a metric so operators can see when circuits open.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that a circuit breaker trips open after too many failures so calls fail fast, Resilience4j runs it as a CLOSED-OPEN-HALF_OPEN state machine over a sliding window, Retry merely re-attempts transient failures, and by default Retry wraps CircuitBreaker so it wastefully retries the open circuit's CallNotPermittedException unless I reorder them so the breaker is outermost or tell Retry to ignore that exception.

---

keyPoints: Circuit Breaker: Closed -> Open -> Half-Open states
Bulkhead: isolate failure to one service pool
Fallback: degrade gracefully when dependency fails
